title: Sorry to the haters but Nicholas Christopher is a star #JustInTime #B...
transcript: At just in time last night, there was an older woman behind us who was a big fan of Bobby Darin. She had never seen the show before, and during intermission, she asked me and my friend Melanie why there were so many young people in the audience super excited about Bobby Darin. Because from her perspective, she grew up with Bobby Darin's music, but the younger generation really doesn't know who he is. And we explained, like, oh, no, we're here for Nicholas Christopher, who just started. And I think a lot of people here are really excited to see him specifically, even if they don't really know Bobby's music. And then at one point during Act 2, she literally leans down to us and says, I see why you guys were so excited to see him. He's very good. And I think the fact that he was able to win over this lifelong Bobby Darren fan is really just a testament to how great a pick he was for this role. He's been this star on the rise for the past couple of years in shows like Sweeney Todd, Little Shop of Horrors, Chess. But in this show, we get to see a completely different side of him. He gets to be this charming, charismatic showman rather than, you know, a murderous barber or a stoic Russian. And vocally, oh, my god, he is opting up. He is adding riffs and runs, and they even let him hold A long note, just like he did in chess. In fact, if you're a chess fan, there's a few fun chess references throughout. And that's the fun thing about Just in Time is every Bobby Darin begins the show as themselves, which gives Nick the opportunity to showcase a little bit of his personality, reference his past work like chess, talk about his upbringing in the Bahamas. He actually had a great joke at the top where he says, I know what you're thinking. Bobby Darin wasn't… bald, but then goes on to point out that he actually was bald and wore a hairpiece. And so in that aspect, he's actually pretty authentic casting. But he does also more directly address the fact that he is a black man playing Bobby Darin, and talked about how Bobby was inspired by a lot of black artists and even marched in Washington alongside Dr Martin Luther King, which I didn't even realize. He also added a line later in the show when Bobby is ripping off some of Elvis's music, and he basically says, hey, don't look at me, Elvis stole it first from Little Richard. And I really love that they used this casting as an opportunity to spotlight some of these black performers who often do not get as much credit as the white performers who borrowed heavily from them. But besides that, the rest of the script is basically the same, including a line in Act 2 where Bobby tells Sandra Dee That he spends more time on his hair than she does. Which obviously is now delivered in a very different context. But the show remains as fun and delightful as ever. And I just keep coming back to that conversation with that older woman as I think it really gets to the heart of what makes Just in time so special. It's not only catering to the older generation who grew up with Bobby's music, but also exposing this whole new generation of theater fans who came to the show because they're big fans of Jonathan Groff or Jeremy Jordan or Nick Christopher or Ariana Madix, who then leave with this appreciation of who Bobby was and his music. There's just something really magical about that to me, and probably why I keep coming back to the show time after time.
classificationReason: Creator explicitly attended ('At just in time last night') and shares a detailed first-hand opinion praising Nicholas Christopher's star-making performance in the show.
